chapter: Technique, jam sessions, audiences and records
title: Fraudulent record companies and lost 1949 records
summary: Smith says most small record men were frauds who vanished, and he found his own records on jukeboxes; he cut a 1949 session with Cooper and never was paid.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: These little recording companies that you recorded, were they offshoots of the big companies like Decca and Columbia and all those, or were they local recording companies?

No, no. All them went under the headin' of some of them big recording companies around the country. And see, some of them was frauds. The big majority of them was frauds. The band was (?)moving on(?) recording, and they listened to them, and the union got behind them and said, "Now, if you don't come up with them contracts and bring them down to the union, and see if you're going to get your money." Well, some of them guys
Buster Smith - 128

that claimed to have this recording done for big companies, when you'd get on the right track and see what's happening, you wouldn't see them no more. They'd disappear. That's happened thousands and thousands of times.
You mean that you'd record with the promise of money, and then the guy would disappear and you'd never see them.

Yeah. When you want to sign his name down, where he's got to pay the band, he'd disappear. Then sometimes you'd go and take a chance with them and make a record, and he'd take the tape or somethin' or nother or a record or somethin' or nother, and go (?) a little business ...(?)., but by then you wouldn't see him no more. And you would hear where he's located and send somebody there to try to catch him or usually write to him...somebody would see him somewhere. He'd say, "Well, the record never did do no good. That's the reason I didn't never come back. It didn't do no good. It didn't bring nothin'." Then I'd be traveling and going through some town, going through to play a date, and get there, and the first thing I'd see on the jukebox is my record playing in there -- the record that I'd just made. See, he wasn't bringin' them to the tavern(?) where you'd hang out at. He'd get some other tavern, or some other city for that matter.
Can you think of any particular record that happened to?
No... Oh, let me see. I found different names of
Buster Smith - 129
different kinds of companies. I'd never heard of them before.
See, the thing is that it's very hard to find records with you on them.
Yes. Uh-huh.
Now, you're suggesting that you did make other records which have just disappeared completely.
Yes.
Did you make a lot of records?
I made quite a few. Quite a few. Right here in Dallas.
In the 30's or in the '40s?

Yeah, in the '40s. Let me see. One I played at (?), and Cooper is on that record with me. We went back to the man and he said the record never did anything, and then I kept on writing, and they said the man didn't work there no more that had come down here... We didn't go to (?) when we made it down there, we thought he was working.

Then I had a bunch of records sent to me around '49(?) from California. They all got away. I had a whole stack of them. A friend of mine, he's dead now, named Fulbright. And sent a whole box to me here, right here at this house, here... And they all got away from me, and I had one. See, I run up on somebody the other month who said they had one of my records. And Buster was singing on it on one side. It was one of them hot records. My
Buster Smith - 130
own original numbers I made up, on both sides. I did have one of (?), but I can't find it. When my wife put stuff away, I never would be able to find it. But the band was jumping, too.
Really.
Yes. Big band.
This was a recording made in the '40s?
The '40s, yeah. '49. Yeah, I made it in '49.
